youtube.description: In this episode you will build paths with pathlib, read, write and list files and avoid hard-coded paths, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Paths as objects · 1:06 Path objects · 1:50 Build, do not type · 2:28 Second program · 3:31 Recap · 4:01 Bug of the Day · 4:49 Challenge · 5:09 Next episode

scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Pathlib gives you a Path object for every file and folder. Join pieces with the slash operator, and Python uses the right separator for the computer it is running on. A Path can tell you its name, its stem, its suffix and its parent. It can check if it exists, read text, write text, and list the files in a folder with glob. Think of a street address that works on every map, built from pieces. Never write a full path like C colon backslash Users by hand. It breaks on another computer.

scenes.narration: [HL 1] Import Path. [HL 3] A path to a file. [HL 4] Does it exist? True. [HL 5] The stem is the name without the extension. The suffix is the extension. Notes, and dot txt. [HL 6] Read text gives the content in one step, with no open and no close. Two lines. [HL 7] The slash operator joins pieces, so the separator is always right for your computer. [HL 8] As posix shows the path with forward slashes, the same everywhere. [HL 9] The parent is the folder. The name is the last part.

code.source:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("notes.txt")
print(p.exists())
print(p.stem, p.suffix)
print(p.read_text().splitlines())
log = Path("data") / "log.txt"
print(log.as_posix())
print(log.parent.name, log.name)

scenes.onScreen: Folder pieces snap together into a path; a Windows computer and a Linux computer each use their own separator
scenes.animation: Folder blocks labelled data and log.txt snap together with a slash symbol; two computers show different separators from the same code
scenes.narration: Here is the idea. You never write the separator yourself. You give Path the pieces, and the slash operator joins them. On Windows, Python joins with a backslash. On Mac and Linux, with a slash. The same code works on both. A path typed by hand works on one computer only. An example is C colon backslash Users backslash Asha. It often works for one person only.

lines: You never write the separator yourself.

A dot txt has three, b dot txt has five. [HL 6] A new path inside the folder. [HL 7] Write text creates the file. [HL 8] It exists now. True. [HL 9] Iterdir lists everything in the folder. Now there are three files.

code.source:
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("data")
for f in sorted(folder.glob("*.txt")):
    print(f.name, f.stat().st_size)
out = folder / "new.txt"
out.write_text("hello")
print(out.exists())
print(sorted(p.name for p in folder.iterdir()))
